full_judgment:
Mr. A.K.M. Shahidul Huq, J: On application at the instance of the petitioner as rule Nisi has been issued to show cause as to why they should not be directed to regularize/absorb the service of the petitioner serving as Data Entry operator of the Development Project namely RLP of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) to the Revenue Budget of the BRDB under the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of his joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of SRO namely “উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের ও নিয়মিতকরন ও জ্যেষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” contain in Memo SRO No. 182/Ain/2005/ Somo/Bidhi-1/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 (Annexure-G) issued by the office of the respondent No.2 under by the Order of the Hon'ble President of the Republic which they are permitted/required by law to do and/or such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Relevant facts for disposal of the rule are that the petitioner is law abiding permanent citizen of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. He has been serving various development project of BRDB Data Entry Operator. The petitioner was firstly appointed under Development Project of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board as BRDB to the posts namely Data Entry Operator vide office Memo No. বাপউবো/পদপএ/ডাটা-এন্ট্রি/নিয়ো/প্রশা-৮৭/৯৪/১৫৫০ dated 05.12.1995. 

The petitioner has been serving the jobs to the BRDB since his appointment with the satisfaction of all concerned. Particularly the Office of the BRDB and also the Office of the Respondent No. 1. As a result the petitioner was transferred from one project to another the petitioner was lastly appointed under the project namely RLP of the BRDB vide office Memo No. বাপউবো/পদপএ/ডাটা-এন্ট্রি/নিয়ো/প্রশা-৮৭/৯৪/১৫৫০ dated 31.7.2013.  

3. Some of the employees of BRDB filed a writ petition being writ petitioner No.7484 of 2009 for regularizing them in revenue head from Development budget. The Division Bench comprising by their Lordships Ms. Justice Naima Haider and Mr. Justice Farid Ahmed vide their judgment and Order dated 17.01.2012 made the rule absolute. The present respondents being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the High Court Division filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal before the Appellate Division but it was dismissed upholding the judgment and order of the High Court Division. 

4. The petitioner stands on the same footing with the employees of BRDB who were earlier absorbed in the revenue head from development budget vide memo NO. বাপউবো/প্রশা/পার/নিয়োগ-১৯৪(১)/২০০০/৭৬২৬ dated 28.7.2005.  

5. The service of employees of various project under the various Ministers were absorbed earlier in the revenue head such as employees of 14 projects under the Ministry Of Social Welfare were absorbed in revenue head. 
6. It is stated that as fresh advertisement of certain employees was published in Daily Samokla dated 10.09.2013 without absorbing the petitioner. It was narrated in that circular that as many as 20 persons would be directly appointed in the revenue budget of the BRDB in that appointment schedule certain educational qualifications were enumerated in that appointment schedule. The petitioner having the same educational qualification as narrated above have been serving in the development project for more than 19 years. The appointment notice had been published instead of absorbing the petitioner in the revenue head in order to deprive the right and legitimate expectations created by the passage of time. It is reveled from the very publications of appointment notice that a lot of posts remained as vacant wherein the petitioner may step in. 

7. There is a Gazette notification issued by the Ministry of Establishment by the order of the Honb'le President of the Country namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” such notification was contained in Memo SRO No.182 Ain/2005 /somo/Bidhi-1S-9/2009 certain Rules were enumerated in that notification by which the employees of the development project are to be transferred to the revenue budget. After absorption their seniority are to be counted from the date of joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of the SRO. 

8. It was seen the respondents were reluctant to count the joining date of the petitioners not from the joining date of the development budget. In such a situation certain persons who earlier absorbed in the revenue head filed a writ Petition No.8983 of 2011 praying for direction to count their joining date form the date of joining in the development budget. The High Court Division initially issued a Rule Nisi and after hearing made the Rule absolute vide judgment and Order dated 14.05.2012. The writ respondents thereafter filed a Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.308 of 2013 against the judgment of the High Court Division. The Appellate Division on 10.03.2013 after hearing was pleased to reject the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal upholding the judgment and Order of the High Court Division. 

9. The petitioner is not challenging the direct appointment process to the post namely Data Entry Operator under the revenue head of the BRDB. But at the same time it is asserted with full knowledge from the Head Office of the BRDB, to the effect that a huge number of the desired posts under the revenue head are vacant. Since the petitioner possessing all the qualifications as required by the BRDB to the appointment to the posts, the petitioner most humbly pray before this Hon'ble Court to pass a direction upon the Office of the respondent No.3 and 4 to keep 1 post vacant till disposal of the Rule. And such claim has already been accepted by some of the employees of the development project of BRDB who filed the writ. petition No.11522 of 2013 and at the time of issuing the Rule such type of Order as prayed in the present writ petition was passed by the High Court Division vide order dated 18.11.2013 in writ petition No.11522 of 2013 and the rule is fixed for hearing on 26.02.2014 for final disposal by this Hon'ble Court. 

10. On perusal of the application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh this Hoh'ble Court issued a rule Nisi. 

11. Mr. Md. Ozi Ullah learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner and Mr. Abdur Rahman appearing on behalf of the respondent No.4. 

12. Mr. Md. Ozi Ullah learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that some employees of the LGRD were absorbed from development budget to revenue budget and the petitioner stands on the same footing with them but he was not taken into the revenue head as such  the respondents adopted the policy of pick and choose and such exercise is illegal, malafide and not tenable under the law as such a direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

13. Learned Advocate next submits that the petitioner has been serving for over 19 years and there was a clear promise from the respondents that the petitioner would be taken into the revenue head and declining such promise is not fair and the petitioner had clear legitimate expectation and such right was sufficiently clear and unambiguous and expressed thus the petitioner must be taken into the revenue head but he was denied by the respondents hence a directions seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required and/or permitted by law to do. 

14. He further submits that Article 27 of the Constitution clearly speaks the equality of all the citizens and are entitled to equal protection of law while Article 31 provides the right to protection of law and they must be treated in accordance with law and only in accordance with law and such is the inalienable right and in the present context the petitioner was not treated in accordance with law and he did not get equal protection of law as because the other employees of the BRDB standing on the same footing with the petitioner were absorbed in the revenue budget from the development budget as such a direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

15. The learned Advocate further submits that the respondents being the public authority must act fairly and justly and not in violation of the law and equity and in the present case the petitioner was the worse victim of the misuse and abuse of the power by the respondents and he was not treated in accordance with law and the petitioner was supposed to be absorbed in the revenue budget but the respondents declined to do so therefore direction is seriously required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to regularize or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 

16. He also submits, a lot of employees of development project of LGRD, Ministry of Education and Jubo Unnayan Adhidoptor were absorbed in the revenue head and furthermore some of the colleagues of the petitioner was absorbed in the revenue head as such a legitimate expectation has not only been created but also matured through various verdicts of the Highest Court and also the Office Memo of the respondent No.4 hence it is seriously required direction is seriously from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents or absorb the service of the petitioner to the revenue head from the development project of BRDB under the Government of Bangladesh which they are required/permitted by law to do. 
17. He lastly submits that there is a Gazette notification issued by the Ministry of Establishment by the order of the Hon'ble President of the country namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫” in which Rule 6 enumerated that the joining date of absorbed employee would be counted the date of initial joining in the development project but such direction was denied hence a writ petition was filed being writ petition No.8983 of 2011 was filed and High Court passed the affirmative decision which was upheld by the Appellate Division in C.P. No.308 of 2013 the said Rule 6 was tested by both the Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh as such along with direction of taking the service from development to revenue head another direction is required from this Hon'ble Court upon the respondents to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of their joining in the development project which they are permitted and/or required by law to do. 

18. The learned Advocate for the petitioner in support of his contention refers the case of Chief Engineer, The Local Government & Engineering Department and others Vs. Kazi Mizanur Rahman & 8 other respondents reported in 17 BLC Appellate Division page 91. 

19. We have heard the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner perused the application filed under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the annexure thereto. In order to arrive at a proper finding it is very much pertinent to refer the case of the Chief Engineer of Local Government and Engineering Department and others Vs. Kazi Mizanur Rahman and 8 others reported in 17 BLC AD page 91 where our Apex Court explained the principle of Legitimate Expectation very elaborately. 

"The doctrine of legitimate expectation is a concept which is akin to that a promissory estoppels and this concept has been developed in the European Community of Law. According to the doctrine where a person is a victim of an unfavorable decision taken by a public authority this may amount to an infringement of that persons legitimate expectation, where for example the decision contradicts an earlier promise or course of conduct on the part of the public authority concerned. Therefore this doctrine is circumscribed by certain limitations and expectations. The first and foremost consideration is that there must be a foundation in the petition claiming legitimate expectation and secondly there must be a promise or a representation on the part of the public on the claim of the person aggrieved by the decision. In this connection it will be very much pertinent to reiterate an observation of the Supreme Court of India in the case of National Building Construction Corporations Vs. Raghunathan reported in AIR 1998 SC page 2779 held that: 

"Incidentally in this case what question of 'legitimate Expectation' and not raised in the petition and foundation was laid in the pleadings for such a plea advanced before the Court. Strangely the High Court allowed this plea at the stage of argument and allowed the petitions only on the ground of Legitimate Expectation without least realizing that there was hardly any legitimacy in the claim of the respondents. In the absence of pleading and the affidavit of the respondents and support thereof the whole exercise done by the High Court cannot be but be termed to be speculation." 

Supreme Court of India in Food Corporation of India -Vs- Kamdhanu Cattle Food Industries Ltd. reported in 1 SCC page 71 observed: 

"The mere reasonable or legitimate expectation of a citizen in such a situation may not by itself by a distinct enforceable right but, failure to consider and give due weight to it may render the decision arbitrary and this is how the requirement of due consideration of a legitimate expectation forms part of the principle of non-arbitrariness concomitant of the rule of law. Every legitimate expectation is as relevant factor requiring due consideration in a fair decision making process. Whether the expectation of the claimant is reasonable or legitimate in the context is a question of fact in each case. Whenever, the question arises it is to be determined not according to the claimant perception but in larger public interest wherein other more important considerations may outweigh what would otherwise have been the legitimate expectation of the claimant. A bonafide decision of the public authority reached in this manner would satisfy the requirement of non-arbitrariness and withstand judiciary scrutiny. The doctrine of legitimate expectation gets assimilated in the rule of law and operates in our legal system in this manner and to this extent." 

Similar views were taken by our Apex Court in the case of Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury, reported in 7 MLR AD page 265 which runs as follows:-

"In the case under our consideration no case has been taken made out from the side of the respondents that there was any act on the part of the Government that could have given rise to a legitimate expectation in the respondents to have the enterprise denationalized in their favour. It has already been mentioned that there is nothing in the Gazette notification of September 27, 1982 wherefrom it can be said from the side of the respondents that the same could give rise in the mind of ordinary prudence expectation of some kind including legitimate expectation of having the enterprise denationalized in their favour. The respondents have not been able to make out a case that in rejecting their representation for having the enterprise denationalized they were not treated fairly or in other words they were not treated equally along with others placed in a situation like that of them. The learned Counsel in support of his submission of absence of case of legitimate expectation on the part of the respondents has placed reliance upon the observation and the ratio of the case reported at AIR 1999 (SC), wherein it has been observed: 

"The principle is at the root of the rule of law and requires regularity, predictability and certainty in government's dealing with the public. The rule of law enforces minimum standards of fairness both substantive and procedural."

In this case this Division approved the views taken in the case of Hindustan Development Corporation. The Court will not interfere on the ground of procedural fairness to a person whose interest based on legitimate expectation might be affected. 

On due and proper consideration and the principles as laid down in the case of LGED—vs- Mizanur Rahman, our Apex Court has laid down certain guidelines on the principle of Legitimate Expectation after reviewing all previous judgment and rules in order to settle the principles of law as regards Legitimate Expectation which sum up under: 

I)	Whenever any vacancy in LGED is created in the revenue set up it shall consider for absorption of employees or officers of the development projects within the meaning of Section 2(ga) of the Rules, 2005 if the project in which she/he is working is completed subject to the condition that such employee or officer has requisite qualification for the said post. 

II)	Whenever a vacant post is created in the revenue budget, the LGED shall absorb/transfer any employee or officer form the development project mentioned is Clause (i) to fill up that post in accordance with Rules of 1985 and the ECNEC's decision dated 10th January, 2008. 

III)	An officer or employee shall be absorbed if she was appointed in the development project within the meaning of rule 2(Ka) of Rules, 2005 in accordance with the procedures prescribed for appointment in public employment. 

IV)	An officer or employee must have requisite qualifications for the post in which he is seeking absorption. 

V)	An officer or employee must have continuity service in the project in which he is working. 

VI)	An officer or employee must have satisfactory service record before his case is considered for regularization in the revenue budget. 

VII)	If an officer and employee whose rank and status does not relate to the posts advertised by the impugned notifications on the day of its publications, such officer or employee would not be eligible for consideration for absorption. 

VIII)	The employees and officers who have been working in the development projects mentioned in Clause (I) on monthly pay basis would only be eligible for consideration for I" absorption in the revenue budget. 

IX)	Unless and until vacancies in the revenue budget in the LGED are created the employees and officers of the development project mentioned in clause (I) cannot claim as of right to be absorbed in the revenue budget. 

X)	While considering and selecting an employee or officer of the development project for absorption in the revenue budget, the appointing authority shall maintain strictly the prevailing quota system for employment in the public employment being followed by the Government. 

XI)	The LGED shall consider the case of those working on master roll basis for absorption in the revenue by phases if they have requisite qualifications subject to the availability of vacancies according to their seniority."

	20. On the similar point our Apex Court in the case of Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) represented by its Director General Vs. Md. Mahbub Alam Khan and others held that the High Court Division came to a finding that in order to facilitate absorption of the personnel of development project the Government promulgated SRO No.182-A i n/2005/S homo/Bidhi 1/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 making clear and specific provisions to absorb all the personnel of development projects which started between 9th April, 1972 to 30th June, 1997. In the instant case, the project of the writ-petitioners started in July, 1993 and they are entitled to be absorbed under the revenue budget pursuant to the provisions of that SRO. The High Court Division further held that the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) at its meeting dated 31.12.2001 had taken decision to transfer all the personnel of the development projects expeditiously to the revenue budget and that the decision was circulated by the Planning Division by the memo dated 10.01.2008 asking all concerned to take necessary steps to transfer all completed development projects to the revenue budget. 

	21. The High Court Division considered the case of Bangladesh Vs. Mr. Abul Hossain (2003) BLD (AD) 129 in which this Division held that once a privilege is given to a person on condition of doing any act and if such condition is fulfilled and continues to be fulfilled, such privilege or right cannot be taken away or cancelled without giving a chance of being heard. Therefore, the High Court Division directed the leave-petitioners to absorb or regularize the writ-petitioners in the regular set up of the Local Government and Rural Development and Co-operatives under the leave-petitioners in permanent post as and when vacancy would arise subject to the condition that they are not otherwise disqualified.  

22. In the case of Chairman, Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs. Nasir Ahmed Chowdhury and others reported in 22 BLD (AD) 2002, page 199 which runs as follows:-

It is held that "an expectation could be based on an express promise or representation or by established past action of settled conduct. The representation must be clear and un-ambiguous. It could be a representation to the individual or generally to a class or persons". 

"Every such legitimate expectation does not be itself fructify into a right and therefore it does amount to as right in the conventional sense." 

The High Court Division in arriving its decision in the instant case relying the decisions reported in 1 WLR page 1482, 2 AC 629 and number of reported decisions of All England Reports. 

In the case of Bangladesh Soya Project Ltd. Vs. Secretary, Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief reported in 22 BLD (HD) 2002, page 378 which runs as follows:

"Government is always under an obligation to act fairly and reasonably even where the other party has no legal right in the conventional sense. This is so even in the case of a contract where the Government is one of the contracting parties.

"In the case of Asab Khan and others Vs. The Court of Settlement reported in 23 BLD (HCD) 2003, page 7 which runs as follows: 

"Legitimate expectation is a concept of administrative law which means that an administrative authority cannot abuse its discretion by disregarding undertaking or statement of its intent. Where an action of the administrative authority adversely affects legal right of an individual, duty to act fairly and reasonably is implicit." 

In the case of North South Property Development Ltd. Vs. Ministry of Land and others reported in 52 DLR (2000), page 7 which runs as follows: 

"A case of legitimate expectation would arise when a body by representation or by past practice amount expectation which it would be within its power to fulfill". 

In the case of Rabia Basri and another Vs. Bangladesh Biman and another reported in 52 DLR (2000) page 308 which runs as follows:-

"The petitioner's expectation of being absorbed in the service after satisfactory completion of five years’ service cannot but be said to their legitimate expectation and in all fairness they should be absorbed in their service." 

In the case of M.P. Sugar Mills Vs. State of U.P. reported in AIR 1979 (S.C.) page 621 which runs as follows:-

"Doctrine of promissory estoppels has been variously called 'promissory estoppels; `requisite' quasi estoppels' and 'new estoppels'. It is a principle evolved by equity to avoid injustice and though commonly named 'promissory estoppels', it is neither in the realm of contract nor in the realm of estoppels. The true principle of 'promissory estoppels' seems to be that where one party has by his words or conduct, made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowing or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it, if it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealing which have taken place between the parties, and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not." 

"This observation of Lord Denning clearly suggests that the parties need not be in any kind of legal relationship before the transaction from which the promissory estoppels takes it origin. The doctrine would seem to apply even where there is no pre-existing legal relationship between the parties, but the promise effect a legal relationship which will arise in further". 

"The true promise of promissory estoppels, therefore, seem to be that where one party has by his words or conduct made to the other a clear and unequivocal promise which is intended to create legal relations or effect a legal relationship to arise in the future, knowledge or intending that it would be acted upon by the other party to whom the promise is made and it is in fact so acted upon by the other party, the promise would be binding on the party making it and he would not be entitled to go back upon it." If it would be inequitable to allow him to do so having regard to the dealing which have taken place between the parties and this would be so irrespective of whether there is any pre-existing relationship between the parties or not. The doctrine of promissory estoppels need not be inhabited by the same limitation as estoppels in the street same of the term. It is equitable principle evolved by the Courts for doing justice and there is no reason why it should be given only a limited application by way of defence. There is no reason in logic or principle of promissory estoppels should also not be available as a cause of action it necessary to satisfy the equity. 

In the case of Commissioner of Customs Vs. Monohar Ali reported in 8 BLC (AD) 2003 which runs as follows:-

"The importers having acted on the promise made by the appellants under Section 25A of the Act to accept the price determined by the Government appointed inspectors, the appellants cannot go back on that promise as it was meant to be binding on them". 
In the case of Nurunnessa Vs. Bahar Ali Bepari reported in 1981 BLD (AD) page 91 which runs as follows:-

"Promissory estoppels-Government making promise-promises acting on the promise-No lack of power of the Government to make the promise-Government bound by the promise."

In the case of Central London Property Trust Ltd. Vs. High Tress House Ltd. (i) Denning J. considered the effect of an arrangement made by the parties and concluded. 

"Where parties enter into an agreement which is intended to create legal relation between them and in pursuance of such arrangement one party makes a promise to the other which he knows will be acted on and which is in fact acted on by the promises, the Court will treat the promise as binding on the promisor to the extent that it will not allow him to act inconsistently with it even though the promise may not supported by consideration in the strict sense." 

In another case of Secretary ,Ministry of Industries Nationalized Industries Division Vs. Saleh Ahmed and another and Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation Vs. Saleh Ahmed and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) page 91 where our Apex Court held that:-

"The Government took the decision on agreement to release the mill in question lack of power on the part of the Government so to do is not the plea, rather a belated plea was taken that the decision has been revised by the Government although no such case was made out. Hence applying the aforesaid principle the least that can be said is that the respondents cannot allowed to act inconsistently and the decision to release the mill remains binding on them. The High Court by the writ has enforced this decision "to complete the formalities for transfer of the mill to the petitioner" 

The same principle as settled in 17 BLC (AD) case has been adopted and followed in the case of Golam Kibria (Md) Vs. Bangladesh by the High Court Division. A Division Bench of the High Court Division held that:- 
"The doctrine of Legitimate Expectation is only an aspect which does not give rise to an enforceable right but only provides that the action taken by the authority while dealing with the citizen is not arbitrary. The applicability of the doctrine of legitimate expectation arises when an administrative body by reason of representation of by past practice or conduct aroused an expectation which it would be within its powers to fulfill unless some overriding public interest comes in the way."

The aforesaid decision of the High Court Division has been reported in 65 DLR (2013) page 148. In another unreported case of Md. Mahbub Alam Khan and others vs. Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Local Government Rural Development and Co-operatives, the Division Bench of the Hon'ble High Court Division while deciding the Writ Petition No.7484 of 2009 on 17.01.2012 held that the petitioners cannot be discriminated and the respondents cannot adopt a pick and choose policy. By working for a reasonable period time the petitioners have all acquired, skills and expertise and can legitimately expect that they will be absorbed. Having served for long years and in view of the past practice the petitioners can reasonably expect that they will be absorbed in the revenue budget. In this connection reliance is placed on the case of Attorney General of Hong Kong -Vs- Ng Then Shik 2 AC 629 a leading case on the doctrine of Legitimate Expectation wherein Lord Fraser said:-

"When a public authority has promised to follow a certain procedure it is in the interest of good administration that it should act fairly and should implement its promise so long as the implementation does not interfere with its statutory duty." 

The doctrine of legitimate expectation and its impact in the administrative law has been considered by our court. Explaining the nature and scope of doctrine of legitimate expectation in the case of Bangladesh -vs-Md. Abdul Hossain reported in 2003 BLD (AD) 129. The Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh held that once a privileged is given to a person on condition of doing any act and if such condition is fulfilled such privilege or right cannot be taken away or cancelled without giving a chance of being heard. 

23. Another aspect which needs to be addressed is that as a result of the petitioners continuance in service for substantial period of time have also become over aged and at this stage they are not in a position to complete with others or seek re-employment in some other establishment. The petitioners who are serving for long spells and have the requisite qualification for the job should not be thrown out but their services should be regularized as far as possible. 

24. The respondents are directed to absorb/ regularize the petitioner serving as Data Entry Operator of the Development project namely RLP of the Bangladesh Rural Development Board (BRDB) to the Revenue Budget of BRDP under the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and to count the seniority for the salary and other service benefits including time scale and selection grade of the petitioner from the date of his joining in the development project as per Rule 6 of SRO namely “এই বিধিমালা উন্নয়ন প্রকল্প হইতে রাজস্ব বাজেটে স্থানান্তরিত পদের পদধারীদের নিয়মিতকরণ ও জৈষ্ঠতা নির্ধারণ বিধিমালা, ২০০৫”contained in Memo SRO  No.182/Ain/2005/ somo/Bidhi-I/S-9/2000 dated 20.06.2005 (Annexure-G) issued by the Office  of the respondent No.2 under by the Order of the Hon'ble President of the Republic which they are permitted/required by law to do vacancy arise subject to the condition that they are otherwise not disqualified. 

25. In view of the observation as made above the rule is disposed of without any order as to cost. 

26. Office is hereby directed to transmit a copy of this judgment to the concern authority at once.

End.
